inequality_on_number_line.wrong: Students draw an open circle for 'greater than or equal to', or fill it in for strict inequality, because they don't connect the circle style to the equals sign in the inequality. They also sometimes point the arrow the wrong way, showing x <= 2 as an arrow going right.
inequality_on_number_line.plain: A solid dot means that exact spot is allowed, a hollow dot means it is not, and the arrow points to every value that counts on that side.
inequality_on_number_line.like: Think of a solid dot as a door that is open for that value to walk through, and a hollow dot as a door that is locked right at that spot.

inequality_sign_flip.what: When you multiply or divide both sides of an inequality by a negative number, the direction of the inequality reverses, because negating flips the order of numbers on the number line - what was bigger becomes smaller.
inequality_sign_flip.example: Start with 2 < 5, both true. Multiply both sides by -1: -2 and -5. Now -2 is bigger than -5, so the sign must flip: -2 > -5.
inequality_sign_flip.wrong: Students multiply or divide by a negative and keep the sign the same, so solving -x > 4 they write x > -4 instead of x < -4 - the algebra step feels identical to the positive case, so the flip gets skipped.
inequality_sign_flip.plain: Flipping something onto its opposite side also flips which one used to be bigger. So when you multiply or divide by a negative number, the whole comparison turns around.
inequality_sign_flip.like: It is like a photo negative - whatever was the lightest patch in the photo becomes the darkest patch once the colours invert.

integer_solutions.what: To list the integers that satisfy an inequality, check the boundary numbers themselves - whether they're included depends on whether the inequality is strict or not - then count the whole numbers between or beyond them.
integer_solutions.example: List integers satisfying -1 < x <= 4: -1 is excluded, 4 is included, so the answers are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
integer_solutions.wrong: Students include or exclude both ends the same way, for example writing -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 by including -1 even though the inequality is strict there, because they don't check each end separately against its own sign.
integer_solutions.plain: Look at each end of the range on its own. One end might let its own number count, while the other end might shut its own number out, so check them separately before you list what is between.

integral_meaning.what: An integral hands you back a function whose slope at every point matches the function you started with - it undoes differentiation the way adding undoes subtracting. If differentiating F gives f, then integrating f gives F back (plus a constant), because differentiation only cares about the shape, not the starting height.
integral_meaning.example: Differentiate F(x) = x^2 + 5 and you get f(x) = 2x. Integrate 2x and you get x^2 + c - the +5 is gone from view, but it could be any constant, since it vanished when you differentiated.
integral_meaning.wrong: Students treat integration as a separate rule to memorise (raise power, divide by new power) with no link to differentiation at all, so when asked WHY it works, they describe the procedure instead of the undoing relationship - and get stuck the moment a question asks them to check an answer by differentiating it.
integral_meaning.plain: Working out a slope and then undoing that step should hand you back roughly what you started with. Integrating is that undoing move, so it always ties back to whatever differentiating would have done to get there.
integral_meaning.like: It is like retracing your steps home from a walk - you end up back where you started, except you cannot be totally sure of the exact house number unless someone tells you which one it was.

integrate_by_substitution.what: When the expression is built from an inner function, you rename that inner function u, rewrite everything (including the limits) in terms of u, integrate the simpler thing, and only then you're done - no need to switch back if the limits were changed to u already.
integrate_by_substitution.example: Integral of 2x(x^2+1)^3 dx from x=0 to 1. Let u = x^2+1, so du = 2x dx. When x=0, u=1; when x=1, u=2. Integral becomes integral of u^3 du from 1 to 2 = [u^4/4] = (16-1)/4 = 15/4.
integrate_by_substitution.wrong: Students substitute u into the expression correctly but then plug the original x-limits (0 and 1) into the u-answer instead of converting them, getting a completely wrong number even though the algebra up to that point was right.
integrate_by_substitution.plain: When a sum has a wrapped-up bit inside another bit, give the inside a new short name so the whole thing gets simple enough to add up. If your start and end points were measured in the old name, swap those over too, so you never have to translate back at the end.
integrate_by_substitution.like: Like changing miles into kilometres before you start a journey calculation - if you convert the start and finish points at the beginning, you never have to convert your final answer back.

integrate_expression.what: To integrate a power of x you raise the power by one and divide by the new power - do that to every term, then stick a +C on the end because any constant vanishes when you differentiate.
integrate_expression.example: Integrate 3x^2 + 4x: each term goes up a power and divides by the new power, giving x^3 + 2x^2 + C.
integrate_expression.wrong: The most common slip is forgetting the +C entirely, since it doesn't change the shape of the answer and often isn't checked. Also common: dividing by the old power instead of the new one, or forgetting to raise the power at all and just multiplying.
integrate_expression.plain: Finding the total from a rate means growing each piece's power by one step and shrinking it by dividing by that new bigger number, then remembering there could have been some fixed starting amount hiding that we can't see, so we add a mystery constant to admit that.
integrate_expression.like: Like knowing how fast a tap is filling a bucket but not how much water was already in it before you started watching - you can work out how much got added, but not the total, so you leave a blank for the unknown starting amount.

integrate_powers.what: To integrate a power of x, push the index up by one and divide by that new index - the exact reverse of the differentiation rule that brings the index down and multiplies by it.
integrate_powers.example: Integrate x^3: raise the power to 4, divide by 4, get x^4/4 + c. Integrate x^(-2): raise to -1, divide by -1, get -x^(-1) + c, i.e. -1/x + c.
integrate_powers.wrong: Students divide by the OLD power instead of the new one, turning x^3 into x^4/3. With negative or fractional powers they often forget to raise the index at all, or mishandle the sign - integrating x^(-2) as x^(-1) + c without the minus sign, since the sign flip from dividing by a negative index is easy to miss.
integrate_powers.plain: To undo the shrinking that happens when you find a rate of change, you do it backwards: make the power one bigger, then divide by that new bigger number.

inverse_function.what: The inverse function undoes what the original function does. To find it, write y = f(x), swap x and y so the roles reverse, then rearrange to get y on its own again - that new expression is f^-1(x).
inverse_function.example: y = 3x + 2. Swap: x = 3y + 2. Rearrange: x - 2 = 3y, so y = (x-2)/3. That's f^-1(x).
inverse_function.wrong: Students rearrange first without swapping x and y, so they find x in terms of y but call it the inverse without ever switching the letters - it looks like progress but it's actually just solving for x, not undoing the function. Others swap correctly but then make an algebra slip while rearranging, like forgetting to divide the whole side by 3.
inverse_function.plain: An inverse undoes exactly what the original does. To find it, swap the input and the output, then work out what you'd need to put in now to get the number you used to put in.
inverse_function.like: Like a recipe that turns raw dough into bread - the inverse asks: if I start with a loaf of bread, what set of steps gets me back to raw dough. You have to reverse the whole process, not just relabel it.

inverse_operations.what: Every operation has one that cancels it out completely - add undoes subtract, multiply undoes divide, squaring undoes square root. If a number is stuck to your letter by one of these, doing the opposite operation to both sides removes it while keeping the equation true, because whatever you do to one side you must do to the other or the balance breaks.
inverse_operations.example: x + 7 = 12. Addition is stuck on x, so subtract 7 from both sides: x = 5.
inverse_operations.wrong: Students subtract 7 only from the side that has the x, leaving x = 12, or they apply the inverse operation to one side and a different operation to the other. This survives because when both sides start off looking almost equal (like x + 0 = 5) skipping the second side changes nothing, so the habit never gets tested.
inverse_operations.plain: If a number is glued onto your unknown by adding, taking away, multiplying, or dividing, you can peel it off by doing the exact opposite thing - but you have to do that same peeling to both sides of the balance, or one side gets heavier than the other.
inverse_operations.like: Like a set of old-fashioned kitchen scales - if you take a weight off one side, you must take the same weight off the other side, otherwise it won't balance any more.

like_terms_meaning.what: Terms can only be combined if they are built from the exact same letters raised to the exact same powers - x and x are alike, but x and x^2, or x and a plain number, are different kinds of quantity and can't be merged into one count.
like_terms_meaning.example: In 4x + 3x^2 + 2x, the 4x and 2x are alike (both plain x), but 3x^2 is not, since it's x squared, not x.
like_terms_meaning.wrong: Students combine 4x and 3x^2 into 7x^2 or 7x, treating any term with an x in it as the same kind. This survives because when only one power of x appears in a whole question, the distinction never gets tested, so the false rule 'if it has x, add it' works every time until x^2 turns up.
like_terms_meaning.plain: You can only add or combine things that are actually the same kind of thing. A plain number of somethings and a squared amount of the same thing look similar but are not the same kind of quantity, so they can't be lumped together.
like_terms_meaning.like: Like counting apples and boxes of apples separately - three apples plus two boxes of apples isn't five of anything, because they're not the same kind of item.

limit_h_to_zero.what: Picture two points on a curve joined by a straight line - a chord. Its gradient is a rough estimate of the curve's steepness. As you slide the second point closer and closer to the first, that chord gradient settles down toward one exact number, and that number is the gradient of the curve at that single point - the derivative.
limit_h_to_zero.example: For y = x^2 at x = 1, the chord to x = 1+h has gradient ((1+h)^2 - 1)/h = 2 + h. As h shrinks toward 0 - try h = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 - this gradient goes 2.1, 2.01, 2.001, closing in on 2.
limit_h_to_zero.wrong: Students think you literally set h = 0 from the start, which gives 0/0 and looks like nonsense, so they conclude the whole method is broken or meaningless. The point is that h never actually reaches 0 - you watch where the value is heading, not where it lands, and that's why the algebra has to simplify away the h in the denominator first.
limit_h_to_zero.plain: Imagine measuring how steep a hill is by picking two spots on it and comparing them. If you keep sliding the second spot closer to the first, your steepness guess keeps getting better and better, and it settles on one exact number even though you never quite let the two spots become the same spot.
limit_h_to_zero.like: It is like guessing your speed by looking at how far you travelled in the last hour, then the last minute, then the last second - the shorter the time you check, the closer your guess gets to your speed at that exact instant.

line_through_two_points.what: Find the gradient from the two points using rise over run, then use one of the points with y=mx+c (or point-gradient form) to pin down the full equation.
line_through_two_points.example: Points (1,4) and (3,10). Gradient m = (10-4)/(3-1) = 6/2 = 3. Using (1,4): 4 = 3(1) + c, so c = 1. Equation: y = 3x + 1.
line_through_two_points.wrong: Students compute the gradient correctly but then plug the x and y from the point into the wrong slots, writing something like c = 4/1 = 4 instead of solving 4 = 3(1)+c properly, or they swap which coordinate is x and which is y when substituting. This gives a plausible-looking but wrong c value like y=3x+4.
line_through_two_points.plain: Once you know how steep the line is, you only need one point on it to pin down exactly where it sits, because there is only one line with that steepness passing through that spot.

log_laws.what: Logs turn multiplying into adding, dividing into subtracting, and powers into multiplying out front. That's the whole toolkit - there's no rule for log of a sum or log of a difference, because those don't simplify at all.
log_laws.example: log(20) = log(4x5) = log(4) + log(5). Also log(8) = log(2^3) = 3log(2). But log(4+5) is NOT log(4)+log(5) - log(9) is about 0.954, while log(4)+log(5) is about 0.602+0.699=1.301. Different numbers entirely.
log_laws.wrong: Students see log(a+b) and split it into log(a) + log(b) because it looks like the product rule, especially under time pressure when the shape of the expression matches something they half-remember. It feels like the same move as log(ab), but there is no rule to justify it, and it silently gives a wrong number that often still looks plausible.
log_laws.plain: A log has exactly three tricks: turn a multiply into an add, turn a divide into a subtract, and pull a power down the front. There is no trick for turning an add into anything - if you see a plus sign inside the log, none of the three tricks apply.

match_coefficients.what: Before you can eliminate a variable, its coefficient has to be the same size in both equations. You look at what each equation is multiplied by, and scale one or both so that one letter's numbers line up.
match_coefficients.example: 2x+3y=7 and x-2y=1. Multiply the second equation by 2: 2x-4y=2. Now the x-coefficient is 2 in both equations, ready for elimination.
match_coefficients.wrong: Students multiply only part of the equation - scaling the x-term but leaving the constant on the other side untouched, so x-2y=1 becomes 2x-4y=1 instead of 2x-4y=2. It looks like the coefficients match, but the equation itself is no longer true, so everything built on it afterward is wrong.
match_coefficients.plain: If you scale up one side of a balanced scale, you have to scale up everything on that side by the same amount, or it stops being balanced. An equation is exactly that kind of balance.
match_coefficients.like: It is like doubling a recipe - if you double the flour you have to double the sugar and the eggs too, not just the flour, or the recipe stops being the same recipe.

midpoint_and_distance.what: The midpoint is the average of the x's and the average of the y's - it just finds the point exactly halfway between two points. The distance is Pythagoras in disguise: the gap in x and the gap in y are the two legs of a right triangle, and the distance is the hypotenuse.
midpoint_and_distance.wrong: Students square-root too early, writing sqrt(4^2)+sqrt(6^2) = 4+6 = 10 instead of sqrt(52). Or they leave the answer as a decimal (7.21) when the question asks for exact form, losing marks for a correctly done calculation.
midpoint_and_distance.plain: The point exactly halfway between two places is just the average of how far along and how far up each one is. The distance between them is figured out the same way you'd work out the diagonal path across a rectangular field, using the sideways gap and the upways gap.
midpoint_and_distance.like: It is like meeting a friend halfway between your two houses - you average how far east each house is and how far north each house is to find the meeting spot.

modulus_graph.what: To sketch y = |f(x)|, sketch y = f(x) normally, then flip any part that dips below the x-axis up above it, like folding the paper along the x-axis. The bottom of that fold, where the graph touches or turns, is the vertex.
modulus_graph.example: y = |x - 3| is a V-shape. It touches zero at x = 3 (the vertex), and rises with slope 1 on both sides, since |x-3| can't go below 0.
modulus_graph.wrong: Students draw the plain unfolded graph (like a straight line through zero for y = x-3, dipping below the axis) and forget to reflect the negative part upward, so the graph is wrong below the axis and there's no V at all. They also often place the vertex at the wrong x-value, forgetting it's where the inside of the modulus equals zero.
modulus_graph.plain: Modulus means distance from zero, so it can never come out negative. Whenever a graph would dip below the middle line, that part gets flipped up above it instead, like folding a piece of paper along a ruler.
modulus_graph.like: It is like folding a strip of paper along a table edge - anything hanging below the table gets folded up to sit above it instead.

modulus_meaning.what: The modulus of x, written |x|, is the distance of x from zero on the number line. Distance can't be negative, so |x| strips away the sign and leaves you with the size of the number.
modulus_meaning.example: |5| = 5, and |-5| = 5 too, because -5 is 5 steps from zero, same as 5 is.
modulus_meaning.wrong: Students think |x| means 'make it negative' or confuse it with brackets and just ignore the bars, so |-5| gets left as -5. It also trips people up in equations: they solve |x-2|=3 by only doing x-2=3, missing that x-2=-3 is also valid, and lose half the solutions.
modulus_meaning.plain: How far a number sits from zero doesn't care which side it's on. Five steps left or five steps right, it's still just five steps.
modulus_meaning.like: Think of a lamppost you walk from every day. Whether you walk fifty metres to the left or fifty metres to the right, you've still gone fifty metres.

multiplier_method.what: Every percentage change is one multiplication. A rise of x% means multiply by (1 + x/100). A fall of x% means multiply by (1 - x/100). To undo it, divide by that same number.
multiplier_method.example: A 15% increase multiplies by 1.15. To undo a 15% increase, divide by 1.15, not multiply by 0.85.
multiplier_method.wrong: Students think a 15% increase is undone by a 15% decrease, multiplying by 0.85 to reverse it - this doesn't get back to the start because 15% off the bigger number is more than 15% of the original. They mix up increase and decrease multipliers, using 1.15 when they mean 0.85 or the reverse.
multiplier_method.plain: Growing by a percentage and then shrinking by the same percentage doesn't bring you back to where you started, because the second change is worked out on a different, bigger number.
multiplier_method.like: If your pay goes up ten percent, then next year drops ten percent, you don't end up on your original wage - the drop was ten percent of the bigger number, so you lose more than you gained.

multiply_divide_fractions.what: To multiply fractions, multiply the tops together and the bottoms together. To divide by a fraction, flip the second one upside down and multiply instead. Simplify at the end (or cancel early if you can).
multiply_divide_fractions.wrong: Students try to find a common denominator for multiplication like they do for adding, giving a wrong answer such as turning 2/3 x 4/5 into something over 15 with the wrong top. For division, a common error is flipping the first fraction instead of the second, or forgetting to flip at all and just multiplying straight across.
multiply_divide_fractions.plain: Multiplying fractions doesn't need matching bottoms the way adding does - you just deal with tops and bottoms separately.
multiply_divide_fractions.like: If you take two thirds of a portion, and then take four fifths of that, you're shrinking it twice - nothing about that needs a shared size to compare against.

multiply_terms.what: Multiply the numbers together, then multiply the letters together, and stick the results side by side.
multiply_terms.example: 3 times 2x: 3*2 = 6, so answer is 6x. x times x: that's x^2, not 2x.
multiply_terms.wrong: For x times x, they write 2x, treating it like addition (x + x = 2x) instead of multiplication. It survives because x + x and x times x look similarly 'simple' and both feel like combining two x's into one thing.
multiply_terms.plain: Putting two of the same letter side by side means they're being multiplied, not added, so they don't just merge into a bigger version of themselves.

negatives.what: Negatives flip direction: subtracting a negative is the same as adding, and multiplying two negatives gives a positive. The sign rules matter more than the size of the numbers.
negatives.example: 5 - (-3) = 5 + 3 = 8. And (-4) x (-2) = 8, but (-4) x 2 = -8. Two negative signs cancel; one negative sign doesn't.
negatives.wrong: Students see 5 - (-3) and either ignore the second negative and write 2, or they see two minus signs and just make it '-8' by multiplying the numbers instead of adding them. With multiplication, a common one is (-4) x (-2) = -8, treating negatives as always making things more negative rather than tracking that two negatives cancel.
negatives.plain: Taking away a debt is the same as being given money, and two things pulling in the opposite direction can end up pushing the same way.
negatives.like: If you owe someone three pounds and that debt gets cancelled, you're three pounds better off - taking away the negative acted just like adding.

normal_equation.what: The normal is the line at right angles to the tangent, at the same point. Perpendicular lines have gradients that multiply to -1, so take the tangent's gradient, flip it upside down, and change its sign.
normal_equation.example: Tangent gradient at a point is 4. Normal gradient = -1/4. If the point is (2,4): y - 4 = -1/4 (x - 2).
normal_equation.wrong: Students just negate the gradient without flipping it (using -4 instead of -1/4), because 'opposite' feels like it should just mean a sign change, not a reciprocal too.
normal_equation.plain: A line that cuts across another at a perfect right angle doesn't just point the other way, it tilts completely differently - steep becomes shallow, not just downhill instead of uphill.
normal_equation.like: Think of a steep ramp and the flat path that meets it square on - the flat path isn't the ramp flipped upside down, it's a totally different steepness.

nth_term_rule.what: An nth term rule is a formula that tells you what any term in a sequence is, based on its position. Feed in the position number n, and it hands back the value sitting there.
nth_term_rule.example: nth term = 3n + 2. The 10th term means put n = 10: 3(10) + 2 = 32.
nth_term_rule.wrong: Students plug the term's value into n instead of its position, or they treat n as if it were the term itself - so asked for 'the term worth 32' they might just write 32 into the formula rather than solving 3n+2=32 for n.
nth_term_rule.plain: A sequence is just a list of numbers in order, and each one has a position in that list, like first, second, third. A rule for the sequence is a little machine: tell it which position you want, and it tells you the number sitting there.
nth_term_rule.like: It is like a row of houses with numbers on the doors - if someone tells you the house number, you know exactly which one to walk to, without checking every house before it.

null_factor.what: If two things multiply together and the answer is zero, one of them has to be zero - there's no other way to make a product vanish. So each bracket can be set equal to zero on its own.
null_factor.example: (x - 3)(x + 2) = 0. Either x - 3 = 0, giving x = 3, or x + 2 = 0, giving x = -2.
null_factor.wrong: Students try to expand the brackets first and then solve, which works but is slow and error-prone, or worse, they set the whole expression equal to zero and try to isolate x directly without splitting into cases, getting stuck or finding only one solution because they never separated the two factors.
null_factor.plain: If you multiply two things together and end up with nothing, then one of them must have been nothing to begin with. There is no other way to get nothing out of a multiplication.
null_factor.like: Like leaving a shop having spent nothing. If the number of items times the price came to nothing, then either the price was nothing or you took nothing home - there is no third way it happens.

optimisation.what: You turn a real situation into a single-variable function using whatever constraint links the variables, then differentiate that function to find the best value - the maths only starts once the setup is done.
optimisation.example: A rectangle has perimeter 20, so x + y = 10, meaning y = 10 - x. Area A = xy = x(10-x) = 10x - x^2. dA/dx = 10 - 2x = 0 gives x = 5, so y = 5 and max area = 25.
optimisation.wrong: Students try to differentiate A = xy directly while it still has two variables, getting nonsense like dA/dx = y. Others substitute the constraint correctly but forget to check the stationary point is actually a maximum, sometimes reporting a minimum or a boundary value as the answer.
optimisation.plain: Before you can find the best possible size or amount, you need to describe the whole situation using just one changing number instead of two, because you can only hunt for a peak or dip when there is a single thing going up and down.
optimisation.like: It is like adjusting only the width of a garden bed once you know the fence length is fixed - the length is forced to change automatically as the width changes, so really you are only turning one dial, not two.

order_fdp.what: To compare a mix of fractions, decimals and percentages, get them all into the same outfit first, usually decimals, then line them up by size.
order_fdp.wrong: Students compare the numbers as they look on the page, so 3/5 gets judged by the digit 5, 0.4 by the digit 4, and 45% by the digit 45, leading to nonsense orderings like putting 45% above 3/5 because 45 is bigger than 5. It survives because with easy numbers like 1/2, 0.5, 50% there is nothing to get wrong.
order_fdp.plain: Fractions, decimals and percentages are three different costumes for the same numbers. Before comparing sizes, change them all into the same costume so comparing them actually means something.
order_fdp.like: It is like comparing prices in pounds, dollars and euros - you cannot tell which is cheapest by staring at the digits, you have to convert them all to the same currency first.

pair_of_unknowns.what: One equation with two unknowns has infinitely many pairs of values that work - you can't pin down x and y from it alone. A second, different equation cuts that down to exactly one pair. The answer isn't 'a value for x' and separately 'a value for y' - it's one matched pair that makes both equations true at the same time.
pair_of_unknowns.example: x + y = 5 alone is satisfied by (1,4), (2,3), (0,5), endless options. Add x - y = 1: now only x=3, y=2 satisfies both. That pair is the answer, not any x and y found separately.
pair_of_unknowns.wrong: Students solve one equation for x, then plug some other value into the second equation to find y without checking the two answers actually satisfy the first equation too, ending up with a 'solution' that only works in one of the two original equations. They treat it as two separate one-line puzzles rather than one shared answer.
pair_of_unknowns.plain: One equation with two unknown numbers has loads of pairs that make it true, so it cannot tell you exactly what the numbers are. A second, different equation narrows it down until only one pair of numbers works in both at once.
pair_of_unknowns.like: It is like knowing two friends' ages add up to thirty - that alone leaves many possibilities, but if you also learn one is five years older than the other, only one exact pair of ages fits both facts.

parametric_diff.what: When x and y are both written in terms of some other letter like t, you find dy/dt and dx/dt separately, then divide one by the other to get dy/dx - the parameter cancels like it would in a fraction.
parametric_diff.example: x = t^2, y = 2t. dx/dt = 2t, dy/dt = 2. dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 2/(2t) = 1/t.
parametric_diff.wrong: Students divide the wrong way round, computing dx/dt over dy/dt instead, getting t instead of 1/t - this survives because both look like plausible answers and nothing in the question flags which is upside down. Others try to eliminate t first to get y in terms of x directly, which works sometimes but wastes time and often goes wrong on messier equations.
parametric_diff.plain: Sometimes x and y are not linked to each other directly - instead they are both controlled by a hidden third number changing behind the scenes. To find how y changes compared to x, you first see how each one changes compared to that hidden number, then combine those two changes together.
parametric_diff.like: It is like two clock hands both driven by the same motor - to compare how fast one hand moves against the other, you look at how each one moves against time first, then work out their speeds relative to each other.

percentage_as_decimal.what: A percentage is a number out of 100, so to write it as a decimal you divide by 100, which just shifts the digits two places. Going back, you multiply by 100.
percentage_as_decimal.example: 32% as a decimal: 32 / 100 = 0.32. And 0.07 as a percentage: 0.07 x 100 = 7%.
percentage_as_decimal.wrong: Students move the decimal point the wrong way, turning 32% into 3.2, or turning 0.07 into 0.0007%. This survives because the direction of the shift is easy to guess wrong under pressure, and they rarely check the size makes sense.
percentage_as_decimal.plain: A percent is just a way of saying 'out of a hundred'. Writing it as a decimal is the same amount, just written in a different costume.
percentage_as_decimal.like: Think of it like pence and pounds - 32 pence out of a pound is the same value as 0.32 of a pound, just written differently.

percentage_change.what: To change an amount by a percentage, work out what that percentage is worth, then add it on or take it off the original amount.
percentage_change.example: Increase 60 by 20%: 20% of 60 is 12, so new amount is 60 + 12 = 72.
percentage_change.wrong: Students find the percentage correctly but forget to add or subtract it, giving 12 as the final answer instead of 72. Others use the wrong original amount when the question involves several changes, working the second percentage off the first result's percentage rather than off the whole new amount.
percentage_change.plain: Changing something by a percentage means working out how big that slice is, then either piling it on top of what you started with or taking it away.
percentage_change.like: Like adding a tip onto a restaurant bill - you work out the tip amount first, then add it to the bill to get what you actually pay.

percentage_of_amount.what: A percentage is a chunk out of 100, so to find it of an amount you turn the percentage into a fraction or decimal of 100 and multiply by the amount.
percentage_of_amount.wrong: Students divide the amount by the percentage number instead of multiplying, so for 15% of 60 they do 60 / 15 = 4. This looks plausible because it gives a smaller number, and often goes unnoticed on percentages under 50.
percentage_of_amount.plain: Finding a percentage of something means working out what fraction of it that percentage represents, then shrinking the whole amount down to that fraction.
percentage_of_amount.like: Like a shop discount - 15% off sixty pounds means working out that slice of sixty pounds, which is the amount you save.

perpendicular_gradients.what: Two lines are perpendicular when their gradients multiply to give -1 - so to find the perpendicular gradient, flip the original fraction upside down and change its sign.
perpendicular_gradients.example: Gradient is 2 (which is 2/1). Flip it: 1/2. Change sign: -1/2. Check: 2 times -1/2 = -1. Correct.
perpendicular_gradients.wrong: Students just change the sign and forget to flip - turning gradient 2 into -2 instead of -1/2. It survives because 'change the sign' is the part people remember, and for a gradient like 1, flipping does nothing, so -1 for '1' happens to be right and reinforces the shortcut wrongly.
perpendicular_gradients.plain: Turning a line through a right angle does two things to its steepness. It swaps how far across for how far up, and it flips which way the line leans. So a gentle climb becomes a steep drop.

perpendicular_line.what: Perpendicular lines have gradients that multiply to give -1, so to get the perpendicular gradient, flip the original gradient upside down and change its sign. Then use the given point to find the equation as usual.
perpendicular_line.example: Line y = 2x + 3, perpendicular through (4,1). Original gradient 2, so perpendicular gradient = -1/2. Using (4,1): 1 = -1/2(4) + c, 1 = -2 + c, c = 3. Equation: y = -1/2 x + 3.
perpendicular_line.wrong: Students flip the sign but forget to also flip the fraction (or vice versa), turning gradient 2 into -2 instead of -1/2. The resulting line looks reasonable and even passes through the given point, so the error only shows up if someone checks the two gradients actually multiply to -1.
perpendicular_line.plain: Before you can write the equation of a line that meets another at a perfect right angle, you need its steepness - and that steepness is the original one flipped over and sent the opposite way.

place_value.what: A digit is worth more or less depending on where it sits, not just what it says. Moving right of the decimal point, each spot is worth ten times less than the one before it: tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths.
place_value.example: In 4.06, the 4 is worth 4 whole ones, the 0 is worth 0 tenths, and the 6 is worth 6 hundredths - so the number is 4 + 0/10 + 6/100.
place_value.wrong: Students see 4.06 and read the digits after the point as '06', treating it like a two-digit number bolted onto the end, so they think 4.06 is bigger than 4.3 because '06' looks bigger than '3'. They're comparing the digits as if position doesn't change what they're worth.
place_value.plain: Where a digit sits changes what it's worth, not just what number it happens to be. The further right you go past the point, the smaller each spot's value gets.
place_value.like: Like pounds and pence - the pounds digit and the pence digit can both be a 6, but one of them is worth far more than the other because of where it sits.

polynomial_division.what: Dividing a cubic by a linear factor works like long division with numbers - you divide, multiply back, subtract, and bring down the next term, ending up with a quadratic (and maybe a remainder).
polynomial_division.example: (x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6) divided by (x-1) gives x^2 - 5x + 6, with no remainder.
polynomial_division.wrong: Students get the sign wrong when subtracting during the process, so terms that should cancel don't, and the quotient comes out with the wrong middle coefficient - here getting x^2 + 5x + 6 or similar because a minus was dropped partway through.
polynomial_division.plain: When you split a big number by a smaller one using long division, you divide, multiply back, subtract, then bring the next digit down. Dividing a messy expression by a simple one works the exact same way, step by step.
polynomial_division.like: It is like sharing out a big pile of sweets bag by bag, checking what is left over after each round before moving to the next batch.

power_of_a_negative_term.what: When you raise a whole term like -2x to a power, everything inside gets raised - the number, the sign, and the letter all together. The sign that comes out depends on whether the power is odd or even, not on what sign you started with.
power_of_a_negative_term.example: (-2x)^3 = (-2)^3 * x^3 = -8x^3. But (-2x)^4 = (-2)^4 * x^4 = 16x^4 - positive, because four negatives multiply to a positive.
power_of_a_negative_term.wrong: Students cube or raise the letter but leave the coefficient as -2 instead of -8, writing -2x^3 instead of -8x^3. Or they assume the answer keeps the original negative sign regardless of the power, so they write -16x^4 for the even case, not noticing the sign should have flipped positive.
power_of_a_negative_term.plain: When something negative gets multiplied by itself, the sign flips each time - so two negatives make a positive, three make it negative again. Whatever you are raising to a power, the sign travels along with the number and the letter together, not just the number on its own.
power_of_a_negative_term.like: It is like flipping a light switch - flip it twice and it is back to how it started, flip it three times and it has changed.

power_of_ten.what: 10 to a positive power is 1 followed by that many zeros. 10 to a negative power is 1 divided by that many zeros' worth of ten, so it's a small decimal. Multiplying by 10^n shifts the decimal point n places - right if n is positive, left if n is negative.
power_of_ten.wrong: Students treat a negative power as a negative number, saying 10^-3 = -1000, because the minus sign in the exponent gets read the same way as a minus sign anywhere else in a sum.
power_of_ten.plain: A power of ten just tells you how far to slide the decimal point. A big positive power slides it right, making the number huge; a negative power slides it left, making the number tiny - it does not make the number negative.
power_of_ten.like: Think of it like zooming a map in or out - zooming out shrinks things down small, it does not flip them upside down.

power_rule.what: To differentiate a power of x, bring the power down in front as a multiplier and knock the power down by one. This works for any power - negative, fractional, whatever - as long as it's written as x to a power.
power_rule.example: y = 3x^4 - 2x^-1 + x^(1/2) dy/dx = 12x^3 + 2x^-2 + (1/2)x^(-1/2) (each term: multiply by old power, subtract 1 from power)
power_rule.wrong: They apply it fine to whole number powers like x^3 but freeze on x^-2 or sqrt(x). For sqrt(x) they often forget to rewrite it as x^(1/2) first, so they either leave it undifferentiated or guess the derivative is (1/2)sqrt(x). For 1/x^2 written as x^-2, they multiply by -2 but then flip the sign of the power the wrong way, landing on -2x^-3 becoming +2x^-1 or similar sign slips.
power_rule.plain: There is one steady move for turning a power of a letter into its rate of change: bring the power down to the front, then lower the power by one. It works whether that power is a whole number, a negative one, or a fraction.

product_rule.what: When two functions are multiplied together, you can't just differentiate each one and multiply the results. Differentiate the first, keep the second as it is, add that to the first kept as it is times the derivative of the second.
product_rule.wrong: The instinctive wrong move is to differentiate both factors and multiply them, giving dy/dx = 2x*cos(x) for the example above. It survives because it feels like the 'obvious' extension of single-function rules, and students never check it against a case where the two answers actually differ, like x=pi/2, where the real derivative and the wrong one give different numbers.
product_rule.plain: When two changing things are multiplied together, their combined rate of change is not just their two rates multiplied. You have to let each one take its turn changing while the other one sits still, then add the two results together.
product_rule.like: It is like a rectangle where both the width and the height are growing - the area grows partly because the width grew and partly because the height grew, and you need both parts added together, not just multiplied.

quadratic_sign_between_roots.what: A quadratic's sign only changes at its roots, so between two roots it's one sign the whole way through, and outside them it's the other sign - which one is which depends on whether the curve opens upward or downward.
quadratic_sign_between_roots.example: Roots at x=-1 and x=4, curve opens upward (U-shape). Below the curve is negative, so between the roots (-1 < x < 4) it's negative, and outside (x < -1 or x > 4) it's positive.
quadratic_sign_between_roots.wrong: Students assume 'between the roots' always means positive, giving -1 < x < 4 as where it's positive when actually the upward-opening shape makes that region negative - they picture a downward curve or just guess without checking which way it opens.
quadratic_sign_between_roots.plain: A curve only crosses from positive to negative right at the points where it touches zero. So between two crossing points it stays one sign the whole way, and outside them it stays the other sign - which is which depends on whether the curve is shaped like a smile or a frown.
quadratic_sign_between_roots.like: It is like a rollercoaster track crossing ground level twice - between those two crossings it dips below ground, and outside them it rises above, depending on which way the track curves.

quotient_rule.what: For one function divided by another, differentiate the top times the bottom, subtract the top times the derivative of the bottom, then divide the whole thing by the bottom squared. Order matters because subtraction isn't symmetric.
quotient_rule.wrong: Students often get the rule mostly right but swap the order of subtraction on top, writing [x^2(1) - 2x(x+1)] / (x+1)^2, which gives the negative of the correct numerator. Because both versions look 'balanced' and use all the right pieces, it's easy to write the wrong order and not notice, especially under time pressure.
quotient_rule.plain: When one changing thing is divided by another, there is an exact order you subtract in, and swapping that order flips the sign of your answer.
quotient_rule.like: It is like working out who owes who money after a split bill - getting the order backwards turns a debt into a credit.

radians.what: Radians measure angles using the radius of a circle instead of degrees - a full turn is 2*pi radians instead of 360 degrees. Calculus and most real-world formulas involving angles want radians, not degrees, because the maths only comes out clean that way.
radians.example: 180 degrees = pi radians. So 90 degrees = pi/2, and 60 degrees = pi/3. To convert 45 degrees to radians: 45 * (pi/180) = pi/4.
radians.wrong: Students leave their calculator in degree mode when a question needs radians (or vice versa), getting numbers that are wildly off but not obviously wrong-looking, since both modes give 'a number'. It survives because most early-level questions don't force the distinction, so the habit of not checking mode never gets punished until it matters.
radians.plain: There is a second way to measure angles that does not use degrees at all, and most maths tools quietly expect you to be using it.
radians.like: It is like a recipe written in millilitres when your measuring jug only shows cups - same amount, wrong units, wrong answer.

ratio_meaning.what: A ratio like 2:3 says for every 2 of one thing there are 3 of the other - it's about the split between them, not the total. Add the parts to find out how many equal shares the whole thing is cut into.
ratio_meaning.example: In a ratio of 2:3, there are 2 + 3 = 5 parts total. If the total is 20, each part is 20/5 = 4, so the amounts are 8 and 12.
ratio_meaning.wrong: Students read 2:3 as meaning 2 out of 3, treating it like a fraction of the whole and getting shares that don't add up properly. Others assume the ratio gives the actual amounts directly, saying the two quantities simply are 2 and 3 regardless of what total the question gives.
ratio_meaning.plain: A ratio tells you how something is split between groups, not how many things there are in total.
ratio_meaning.like: It is like sharing sweets between two friends by handing out two, then three, then two, then three - the pattern tells you the split, not the total bag size.

rationalise_denominator.what: A surd sitting under a fraction line is considered 'untidy', so you multiply top and bottom by something that turns that surd into a whole number, without changing the value of the fraction since you're really multiplying by 1.
rationalise_denominator.example: Simplify 3/sqrt(2). Multiply top and bottom by sqrt(2): (3*sqrt(2))/(sqrt(2)*sqrt(2)) = (3*sqrt(2))/2.
rationalise_denominator.wrong: Students multiply only the denominator by sqrt(2) and forget the numerator, turning 3/sqrt(2) into 3/2 and losing the sqrt(2) entirely, or they multiply by sqrt(2)/sqrt(2) correctly but simplify sqrt(2)*sqrt(2) as 2sqrt(2) instead of 2.
rationalise_denominator.plain: A square root sitting on the bottom of a fraction is seen as messy, so there is a trick to move it to the top without changing what the fraction is worth.

rearrange_formula.what: Making a letter 'the subject' means getting it alone on one side of the equals sign, using the same moves you'd use to solve an equation - whatever you do to one side, you do to the other, undoing operations in reverse order.
rearrange_formula.example: C = 2 pi r, make r the subject. Divide both sides by 2 pi: C/(2 pi) = r. So r = C/(2 pi).
rearrange_formula.wrong: Students divide only the C, writing r = C/2 pi meaning C/2 times pi, or they divide by 2 and forget the pi entirely, getting r = C/2. Both come from treating 2 pi as two separate things instead of one multiplied block sitting next to r.
rearrange_formula.plain: Getting a letter on its own means peeling away everything stuck to it, one layer at a time, doing the exact same peel to both sides of the equals sign.
rearrange_formula.like: It is like unwrapping a present - you take off the same layer of tape and paper from both hands at once, not just one.

reciprocal.what: Dividing by a fraction asks how many of that fraction fit into your number. Flipping the fraction and multiplying works because dividing by something small makes the answer bigger, and multiplying by its reciprocal does exactly that.
reciprocal.example: 6 / (1/2) asks how many halves fit into 6, which is 12. Using the rule: 6 x 2/1 = 12, matching the answer.
reciprocal.wrong: Students think dividing always makes numbers smaller, so they expect an answer smaller than 6 and get confused or forget to flip, computing 6 / 1 / 2 = 3 instead, which happens to look plausible because it is still a small clean number.
reciprocal.plain: Dividing by a fraction is really asking how many of that fraction you can fit inside your number, and that answer can end up bigger, not smaller.
reciprocal.like: It is like asking how many quarter-hour slots fit into an hour - the answer is four, bigger than the hour you started with.

recognise_composite.what: A composite function is one built by putting one function inside another - you do something to x, then do something else to the result. To spot one, ask: is there an 'outer' action being applied to a whole 'inner' expression, rather than to x directly?
recognise_composite.example: sin(x^2) is composite: the inner function is x^2, the outer function is sin(). But sin(x) + x^2 is not composite - it's just two separate pieces added together.
recognise_composite.wrong: Students see any expression with two operations in it and call it composite, so they say x^2 + 3x is composite because it has a power and a multiplication. The real test is whether one whole expression is sitting inside another, not just whether there's more than one operation.
recognise_composite.plain: Sometimes one whole calculation gets done to x first, and then a second calculation gets done to that answer, not to x itself. The question is whether something is being done to a full result, rather than two separate things happening side by side.
recognise_composite.like: Think of getting dressed then putting on a coat over the top - the coat goes over the whole outfit, not just over your arm. That's different from wearing a hat and shoes at the same time, which don't sit on top of each other.

recognise_index_form.what: Some expressions look like ordinary numbers or products but are actually powers of the same base in disguise - things like 9, 27, 1/8, or sqrt(2). Before you can add, compare, or solve anything with them, you have to see that 9 is really 3^2 and 27 is really 3^3, so they share a base and can be combined.
recognise_index_form.example: You are asked to solve 9^x = 27. As written you cannot do anything - different bases. Rewrite both as powers of 3: 9 = 3^2, 27 = 3^3. Now the equation is (3^2)^x = 3^3, so 3^(2x) = 3^3, so 2x = 3.
recognise_index_form.wrong: Students try to solve 9^x = 27 directly, sometimes taking logs clumsily or guessing x = 3, because they don't spot that 9 and 27 are both powers of 3. Without that spotting step, the whole method never starts.
recognise_index_form.plain: Some numbers are secretly the same number multiplied by itself a few times, just written differently. Spotting that two different-looking numbers actually come from the same building block is what lets you compare or combine them.
recognise_index_form.like: It is like realising fifty pence, a pound, and two pounds are all just different amounts of the same coin - once you see they all come from twenty pences, working with them gets much easier.

recognise_product.what: A product is two separate functions of x multiplied together, where neither is a fixed number. Spotting one means picking out the two pieces, u and v, that are each doing their own thing with x.
recognise_product.example: x^2 * sin(x) is a product: u = x^2, v = sin(x). But 3 * sin(x) is not a product needing the product rule - 3 is just a constant multiplier.
recognise_product.wrong: Students label anything with a multiplication sign as a product needing the product rule, so they overcomplicate 5x^3 (which is just a constant times a power) by splitting it into u=5, v=x^3 and grinding through unnecessary steps. It still gives the right answer, so the habit never gets corrected.
recognise_product.plain: Sometimes you're multiplying two things that both change depending on x. That's different from multiplying something changing by a plain fixed number - the fixed number doesn't need special treatment.
recognise_product.like: Picture speed multiplied by time, where both are changing as you drive - that's different from doubling a single changing number, like just multiplying your speed by two.

recognise_quotient.what: Some expressions are written as one thing divided by another, but that doesn't mean you must use the quotient rule - if the bottom is just a number or a simple power of x, it's often faster to rewrite it as a product with a negative power.
recognise_quotient.example: x^3 / 5 is easier as (1/5)x^3, a simple power - no quotient rule needed. But (x^2 + 1)/(x - 1) genuinely needs the quotient rule, since both top and bottom vary with x in a complicated way.
recognise_quotient.wrong: Students see a fraction and immediately reach for the quotient rule, even when the denominator is a constant like x/2 or x^3/7, turning a one-line power rule problem into a messy quotient rule calculation - which often still works but wastes time and invites arithmetic slips.
recognise_quotient.plain: When something is divided by a number that never changes, you don't need a complicated rule for division - you can treat it as an easier multiplication instead. Save the harder method for when both the top and the bottom are genuinely changing.
recognise_quotient.like: Splitting a bill three ways is just dividing by a fixed number, so you can do it in one simple step. It's only complicated when the number of people sharing the bill keeps changing too.

recognise_reverse_chain.what: Some integrals are one function stuffed inside another, with the derivative of the inside sitting right there as a factor. If you can see 'a function of a function, times the derivative of the inner bit', that's your signal to substitute u = inner bit.
recognise_reverse_chain.example: Look at the integral of 2x(x^2+1)^5 dx. The inner function is x^2+1, its derivative is 2x, and 2x is sitting right there multiplying the bracket. So substitute u = x^2+1, du = 2x dx, giving integral of u^5 du = u^6/6 + C = (x^2+1)^6/6 + C.
recognise_reverse_chain.wrong: Students try to expand (x^2+1)^5 first with the binomial, or they guess the answer is (x^2+1)^6/6 without checking the 2x was needed - which works here by luck but fails the moment the factor out front isn't the exact derivative, like integral of x(x^2+1)^5 dx where they forget the missing factor of 2.
recognise_reverse_chain.plain: Sometimes a calculation is hiding a smaller calculation inside it, and the rate at which that smaller part is changing is sitting right next to it, multiplied in. Spotting that match is what tells you the two parts belong together.

reverse_percentage.what: When you're given the amount after a percentage change, don't undo it by adding or subtracting the percentage back. Work out what the original was multiplied by, then divide by that.
reverse_percentage.example: After a 20% increase, a price is 72. That's 120% of the original, so original = 72 / 1.20 = 60.
reverse_percentage.wrong: Students take 20% of 72 and subtract it, getting 72 - 14.40 = 57.60 instead of 60. This feels like 'undoing' the increase but percentages don't reverse like that, because the 20% was worked out from the smaller original amount, not from 72.
reverse_percentage.plain: When you already know the amount after something has grown or shrunk by a percentage, you can't get back to the start by adding or taking off that same percentage. You have to work out what single multiplication got you to that amount, then undo that multiplication.
reverse_percentage.like: If your height grew by ten percent last year, taking ten percent off your new height won't get you back to your old height - because that ten percent was worked out from the smaller, old you, not the taller, new you.

rewrite_index_form.what: Roots and fractions are just powers in disguise. A square root is a power of 1/2, and dividing by x to a power is the same as multiplying by x to the negative of that power. Once everything is x to some power, you can use the index laws on it.
rewrite_index_form.wrong: Students leave the root or fraction as it is and try to differentiate or simplify it directly, getting stuck or using the wrong rule entirely - like trying to use the chain rule on 3/x^2 instead of just writing it as 3x^-2 first and using the power rule.
rewrite_index_form.plain: A root sign and a number sitting underneath a fraction are both just powers wearing a disguise. Once you unmask them and write everything as one thing raised to a power, all the old power rules work again.
rewrite_index_form.like: It is like a nickname on a team sheet - once you swap it for the player's real name, all the usual rules about who plays where apply again.

second_derivative.what: Differentiate once to get the rate of change, then differentiate that result again to get the rate of change of the rate of change. The sign of this second result tells you whether the original graph is curving upward like a smile (positive) or downward like a frown (negative).
second_derivative.example: y = x^3 - 3x dy/dx = 3x^2 - 3 d^2y/dx^2 = 6x At x = 2: 6(2) = 12, positive, so curve is concave up there.
second_derivative.wrong: They differentiate once, get dy/dx, and treat that as the answer to a question asking about concavity - stopping a step early because dy/dx also involves derivatives so it 'feels' like the right kind of object. Or they differentiate twice correctly but then read the sign backwards, saying positive means the curve bends downward.
second_derivative.plain: Working out the slope tells you which way the hill is going. Working out the slope of that slope tells you whether the hill is curving into a smile shape or a frown shape.
second_derivative.like: Speed tells you how fast a car is going. Whether the speed is climbing or dropping tells you if the driver is pressing the accelerator or the brake.

set_derivative_zero.what: Stationary points are where the curve is momentarily flat - gradient zero. Once you already have dy/dx, the move is just to write dy/dx = 0; that equation is the thing you solve to find where those points are.
set_derivative_zero.example: dy/dx = 3x^2 - 12. The equation to solve is 3x^2 - 12 = 0.
set_derivative_zero.wrong: Students set y = 0 instead of dy/dx = 0, because they're chasing 'where the curve crosses the x-axis' rather than 'where it's flat' - a different question that happens to look similar.
set_derivative_zero.plain: The flat spots on a curve, where it stops climbing and starts falling or the other way round, happen exactly where the slope is nothing at all. So to find them, you take the formula for the slope and ask when it equals nothing.

share_in_ratio.what: Add up the ratio parts to find how many equal shares there are in total, work out what one share is worth, then give each part its number of shares.
share_in_ratio.example: Share 30 in the ratio 2:3. Total parts = 2+3 = 5. One part = 30/5 = 6. So shares are 2*6=12 and 3*6=18.
share_in_ratio.wrong: They split the amount straight by the ratio numbers without finding one share first, like giving 2 and 3 directly, or dividing 30 by 2 and by 3 separately (15 and 10), which doesn't add back to 30 and ignores what the ratio numbers actually represent.
share_in_ratio.plain: First work out how many equal slices the whole amount gets cut into, then see how big one slice is, then hand out however many slices each person's number says.
share_in_ratio.like: It is like splitting a pizza between people who don't want equal amounts - you cut it into the right number of equal slices first, then give some people more slices than others.

simplify_derivative.what: After differentiating, you often get a messy sum of terms with common factors buried in them - powers of x, brackets, whatever - and the job is to pull those shared factors out front so the expression is one tidy product instead of an addition.
simplify_derivative.example: y' = 3x^2(x-1)^2 + 2x^3(x-1) simplifies by taking out the common factor x^2(x-1): y' = x^2(x-1)[3(x-1) + 2x] = x^2(x-1)(5x-3).
simplify_derivative.wrong: Students leave the derivative as a sum because it's technically already an answer, then can't solve y'=0 from it since a sum of terms doesn't reveal its roots the way a product does. Others try to factor but miss the smaller shared power (pulling out x^3 instead of x^2), leaving a leftover x sitting outside the bracket where it shouldn't be.
simplify_derivative.plain: After you work out a slope formula it often comes out as a messy sum with the same pieces hiding inside each part. Pulling those shared pieces out front turns the mess into one tidy multiplication, which is much easier to work with.
simplify_derivative.like: It is like noticing everyone in a bill ordered the same side dish - instead of listing it separately under each person's total, you pull it out once and multiply.

simplify_index_expression.what: Roots are fractional powers and fractions of powers are subtractions - once everything is written as a single base raised to a single index, you just add, subtract or multiply the indices using the normal power rules.
simplify_index_expression.wrong: Students simplify the whole numbers and the roots separately, or forget to convert the root into a fractional power at all, leaving an answer like x^3 * sqrt(x) / x^2 uncombined, or wrongly cancelling to get x^(1/2) by matching 'x^3 over x^2' and ignoring the sqrt(x) term.
simplify_index_expression.plain: A root sign is a fraction hiding as a power, and dividing powers of the same thing means subtracting how many times it's multiplied. Turn everything into one thing raised to one power, then add or subtract those powers using the normal rules.

simplify_logs.what: Logs turn multiplication into addition and division into subtraction, and a power in front of a log becomes a multiplier out front (or vice versa). Use these three moves to squash several logs into one, or to pull one log apart.
simplify_logs.example: Write 2log(x) + log(y) - log(z) as a single log. 2log(x) = log(x^2). So log(x^2) + log(y) - log(z) = log(x^2 y) - log(z) = log(x^2 y / z).
simplify_logs.wrong: Students try to add the logs first and write log(x) + log(y) = log(x+y), treating log like it distributes over addition the way multiplication does. This is backwards - log(x)+log(y) = log(xy), not log(x+y) - but it feels natural because addition 'should' combine simply.
simplify_logs.plain: When two logs are added together, that actually means the numbers inside them get multiplied. Once you see logs as a code for multiplying and dividing, squashing them together or pulling them apart is just following the code.
simplify_logs.like: It is like two people saying how loud something is in decibels. Adding the decibels is really the same as multiplying how much louder it actually got.

simplify_ratio.what: Divide both sides of the ratio by the same number, over and over, until nothing but 1 divides both parts evenly.
simplify_ratio.wrong: They divide by a number that only works on one side, or stop too early - for 8:12 they might divide by 2 and stop at 4:6, thinking it's simplified because both numbers got smaller.
simplify_ratio.plain: A ratio is just comparing two amounts, so you can shrink both numbers down as long as you shrink them by the same amount each time, right down until they cannot get any smaller.
simplify_ratio.like: It is like a recipe for two people that you scale down bit by bit until you reach the smallest version that still tastes the same.

simultaneous_linear_quadratic.what: The line crosses the curve in up to two places, so you set the two expressions for y (or x) equal to each other, get a quadratic, solve it for two x-values, then find the matching y for each.
simultaneous_linear_quadratic.example: y=x+1 and y=x^2-1. Set them equal: x+1=x^2-1, so x^2-x-2=0, which factors to (x-2)(x+1)=0. So x=2 or x=-1. Using y=x+1: x=2 gives y=3, x=-1 gives y=0. Answers: (2,3) and (-1,0).
simultaneous_linear_quadratic.wrong: Students solve the quadratic and stop there, giving x=2 and x=-1 as 'the answer' without ever finding the matching y-values - because the quadratic felt like the hard part and the question felt finished. Others find y using the quadratic equation instead of the linear one, which technically also works but doubles the arithmetic and invites mistakes.
simultaneous_linear_quadratic.plain: A straight line and a curve can cross each other in two spots, and finding those spots means finding both the sideways position and the up-down position for each one - not just where they line up sideways.
simultaneous_linear_quadratic.like: It is like two people's paths crossing twice in a park. Knowing they cross isn't enough - you need to say exactly where each meeting happened, both how far along and how far up.

sketch_modulus_graph.what: Sketch the graph as if there were no modulus, then take any part that dips below the x-axis and flip it upward, like folding the paper along the x-axis.
sketch_modulus_graph.example: y = |x - 3|. Without the modulus this is a straight line through (3,0) with gradient 1. The part where x < 3 would go negative, so flip that part up - result is a V-shape with vertex at (3, 0).
sketch_modulus_graph.wrong: They draw the plain straight line or parabola and forget to reflect the negative section, so the graph dips below the x-axis where it never should - modulus output can't be negative.
sketch_modulus_graph.plain: Modulus means distance from zero, so it can never come out negative - if the ordinary graph would dip below the line, you flip that bit back up instead.
sketch_modulus_graph.like: It is like a heart rate monitor that only shows speed, not direction - it can't show you going backwards, so any dip below zero gets shown as a bounce upward instead.

solution_is_a_range.what: An inequality doesn't pin x down to one exact spot, it only says x is bigger, smaller, or equal to something - so every number that fits that description is a valid answer, and there are infinitely many of them.
solution_is_a_range.example: x + 2 > 5 gives x > 3. That's true for x=3.1, x=4, x=1000 - all of them at once, so the answer is the whole range x > 3, not a single value.
solution_is_a_range.wrong: Students solve the inequality like an equation, get x = 3, and give that as THE answer - because solving equations trains you to expect one number, and the habit doesn't let go just because the sign changed.
solution_is_a_range.plain: An inequality doesn't point at one number, it points at a whole crowd of numbers that all make it true, stretching off forever in one direction.
solution_is_a_range.like: It's like a sign saying you must be taller than four feet to ride - that doesn't name one height, it lets in everyone above it.

solve_both_sides.what: When x shows up on both sides, get all the x-terms together on one side and all the plain numbers together on the other, moving each term across the equals sign by doing the opposite operation.
solve_both_sides.example: 5x - 3 = 2x + 9. Subtract 2x from both sides: 3x - 3 = 9. Add 3 to both sides: 3x = 12. Divide by 3: x = 4.
solve_both_sides.wrong: Students shift the x-term correctly but forget to flip the sign on the number when it crosses, writing 3x = 9 - 3 = 6, giving x = 2 instead of 4.
solve_both_sides.plain: If x turns up on both sides of the balance, you shift all the x's to one side and all the plain numbers to the other, and every time something hops over the equals sign it switches from adding to taking away, or the other way round.
solve_both_sides.like: It's like sorting two mixed piles of coins and notes between two people until one person only holds coins and the other only holds notes - whatever crosses over changes hands, not what it's worth.

solve_exponential_equation.what: When the two sides of an equation with x in the index can't be forced onto the same base, taking logs of both sides brings x down out of the index so you can solve for it normally.
solve_exponential_equation.example: Solve 5^x = 20. Take logs: log(5^x) = log(20), so x*log(5) = log(20), so x = log(20)/log(5), which is about 1.86.
solve_exponential_equation.wrong: Students try to force 20 into a power of 5 by trial and error and get stuck, or they take the log of only one side, writing x = log(20)/5 instead of x = log(20)/log(5), producing a wildly wrong decimal answer.
solve_exponential_equation.plain: When the unknown number is stuck up in the power position and you can't rewrite both sides using the same base, there's a trick that pulls it back down to normal ground level so you can work with it properly.
solve_exponential_equation.like: It's like a name written up high on a scoreboard that you can't reach - logs are the ladder that brings it down to where you can read it.

solve_index_equation.what: To solve for x in the index, get both sides written as a power of the same base, then the indices themselves become a normal equation you solve like any other.
solve_index_equation.example: Solve 9^x = 27. Write both as powers of 3: (3^2)^x = 3^3, so 3^(2x) = 3^3, so 2x = 3, so x = 1.5.
solve_index_equation.wrong: Students try to solve 9^x = 27 by taking logs straight away or by guessing whole number values of x, missing that x = 1.5 works, since it isn't obvious from trial and error, and often just give up or write x = 3 by dividing 27 by 9.
solve_index_equation.plain: If both sides of the puzzle can be rewritten using the exact same base number, then the powers themselves must be equal, and that gives you a plain, ordinary equation to solve.
solve_index_equation.like: It's like comparing two stacks of the same size box - if the stacks are equal, you only need to count how many boxes are in each.

solve_linear.what: Solving a linear equation means undoing what's been done to x, one step at a time, in reverse order, until x is alone.
solve_linear.example: 3x + 7 = 22. Subtract 7 from both sides: 3x = 15. Divide both sides by 3: x = 5.
solve_linear.wrong: Students divide by 3 first while the +7 is still there, getting 3x/3 + 7 = 22/3, which turns into a mess like x + 7 = 7.33, because they treat 'undo the equation' as 'divide everything by the coefficient' without clearing the addition first.
solve_linear.plain: To find the hidden number, undo everything that was done to it, but undo it in the opposite order to how it was built up.
solve_linear.like: It's like taking off your shoes and coat before bed in reverse order to how you put them on - coat off first, then shoes, not the other way round.

solve_linear_inequality.what: Solve it like an equation, moving terms and dividing as usual, but if you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, the inequality sign flips direction.
solve_linear_inequality.example: Solve -2x + 3 > 7. Subtract 3: -2x > 4. Divide by -2 (flip the sign): x < -2.
solve_linear_inequality.wrong: Students divide by the negative and keep the sign the same, getting x > -2 instead of x < -2. It looks like ordinary equation-solving so the flip step gets skipped, and the answer is backwards.
solve_linear_inequality.plain: You solve it the same way as a normal equation, but there's one extra rule: if you multiply or divide by a negative number, the direction of the inequality has to turn around.
solve_linear_inequality.like: It's like a mirror flipping left and right - once you cross into negative territory, bigger and smaller swap places.

solve_log_equation.what: Get all the logs onto one side, squash them into a single log, then use the fact that if log_b(A) = c, then A = b^c. This turns a log equation into an ordinary equation you can solve, but you must check your answers actually work in the original equation because logs of negative numbers or zero don't exist.
solve_log_equation.example: Solve log2(x) + log2(x-2) = 3. Combine: log2(x(x-2)) = 3. So x(x-2) = 2^3 = 8. x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0, (x-4)(x+2)=0, x=4 or x=-2. Check x=-2: log2(-2) is undefined, reject it. Answer: x=4.
solve_log_equation.wrong: Students solve the quadratic and write down both roots as the answer, because the quadratic-solving step feels like the finish line and they forget logs need positive inputs. On easier questions where both roots happen to be positive this mistake never gets caught, which is why it sticks around.
solve_log_equation.plain: Squash all the logs together into one, then unwrap that single log to get back to an ordinary equation, and always check the answer still makes sense once you're done.
solve_log_equation.like: It's like unlocking a box within a box - once you're inside, you still have to check what you found is actually real and not something impossible.

solve_modulus_equation.what: A modulus equation splits into two cases: the inside expression equals the other side, or the inside expression equals minus the other side. Solve both, then check each answer actually works in the original equation, since a modulus can never come out negative.
solve_modulus_equation.example: |x - 5| = 2x + 1. Case 1: x - 5 = 2x + 1 gives x = -6, but then 2x+1 = -11, negative, and modulus can't equal a negative number - reject. Case 2: x - 5 = -(2x+1) gives 3x = 4, x = 4/3, check: |4/3 - 5| = 11/3 = 2(4/3)+1 = 11/3 - valid. Only x = 4/3 works.
solve_modulus_equation.wrong: They find both x-values from the two cases and give both as final answers without checking whether the right-hand side is actually non-negative at each one, so an invalid extra solution like x = -6 slips through.
solve_modulus_equation.plain: A modulus means the distance from zero, so it could have come from a positive number or its negative twin, meaning you have to check both possibilities and throw out any answer that gives a distance that can't exist.
solve_modulus_equation.like: It's like being told someone walked ten steps from home - they could be ten steps north or ten steps south, so you check both directions before deciding which one actually happened.

solve_quadratic.what: A quadratic usually has two values of x that make it true, and to find both you get everything to one side equal to zero, factorise, then use that each bracket can be zero on its own. If it won't factorise nicely, the formula or completing the square gets you there instead.
solve_quadratic.example: Solve x^2 - x - 6 = 0. Factorise: (x - 3)(x + 2) = 0. So x = 3 or x = -2.
solve_quadratic.wrong: Students find one solution - often just the positive one - and stop, forgetting a quadratic normally has two. This survives because many textbook answers only ask you to 'solve for x' and one root often looks like enough, especially if the negative root seems less obviously relevant to the context of the question.
solve_quadratic.plain: Some equations have two different starting numbers that both end up working, and if you only find one of them, you have only done half the job.
solve_quadratic.like: Like being asked which two floors a lift stopped at - finding the third floor does not mean you can ignore the sixth.

solve_quadratic_inequality.what: Find the roots of the quadratic, sketch the shape of the curve, and use that shape to read off which x values make the inequality true - the answer is one or two ranges, not just the two numbers you found.
solve_quadratic_inequality.example: Solve x^2 - x - 6 > 0. Factor: (x-3)(x+2) > 0, roots at x=3 and x=-2. Curve is a U-shape, positive outside the roots. Answer: x < -2 or x > 3.
solve_quadratic_inequality.wrong: Students solve for the roots x=-2 and x=3 and just write those down as the answer, or write -2 < x < 3 without checking against the shape of the curve - which happens to be exactly backwards here since the parabola is positive outside the roots, not between them.
solve_quadratic_inequality.plain: The two numbers you find are not the answer here - they are the fence posts. You then need to work out which side of the fence, or which patch of ground, the question is actually asking about.
solve_quadratic_inequality.like: Like being told a shop is open before nine and after five - the opening times mark the gaps, they are not the answer to when it is open.

solve_simultaneous_elimination.what: You've got two equations, two unknowns, and neither variable lines up neatly. So you scale one or both equations up until one variable has matching (or opposite) coefficients, then add or subtract the whole equations to wipe that variable out.
solve_simultaneous_elimination.example: 3x+2y=16 and x+y=6. Multiply the second by 2: 2x+2y=12. Subtract this from the first: (3x+2y)-(2x+2y)=16-12, giving x=4. Put x=4 back into x+y=6: y=2.
solve_simultaneous_elimination.wrong: Students multiply only the equation they're 'working on' and forget the other side of the equals sign, or multiply one equation but not scale the y-term the same way - so they might turn x+y=6 into 2x+y=12 (only doubling x). The coefficients then don't actually match, and subtracting gives a wrong value that still looks like a clean number, so it slips through unnoticed.
solve_simultaneous_elimination.plain: When you scale up one equation to make things match, you have to scale up every single part of it, including the number on its own, not just the letters you are focused on.
solve_simultaneous_elimination.like: Like doubling a recipe - if you double the flour and the eggs but forget the sugar, the whole thing goes wrong even though most of it looks doubled.

solve_simultaneous_substitution.what: Get one equation to say 'y equals something' (or x equals something), then swap that something into the other equation wherever that letter appears. That turns two equations with two unknowns into one equation with one unknown, which you can actually solve.
solve_simultaneous_substitution.example: y = x + 1 and 2x + y = 7. Substitute: 2x + (x+1) = 7, so 3x + 1 = 7, 3x = 6, x = 2. Then y = x+1 = 3. Check: 2(2)+3 = 7, correct.
solve_simultaneous_substitution.wrong: Students substitute into the same equation they got the expression from, going in a circle and getting 0=0 or something meaningless. Or they substitute correctly but forget the brackets, writing 2x + x + 1 = 7 as 2x + x1 = 7 or dropping the +1 halfway through, so they get x = 3 instead of x = 2.
solve_simultaneous_substitution.plain: Once you know what one letter equals in terms of the other, you swap it into the other equation, not back into the one it came from - that second move just brings you back to where you started.

solve_with_brackets.what: A bracket means everything inside gets multiplied by whatever sits outside it, so that has to happen before anything else to the equation.
solve_with_brackets.wrong: Students multiply only the first term inside the bracket, turning it into 3x + 2 = 21, and solve from there to get x = 19/3, which is wrong because the 2 never got multiplied by 3.
solve_with_brackets.plain: Whatever sits right outside a bracket has to be shared out to everything inside it, not just the first thing it happens to touch.
solve_with_brackets.like: Like paying for everyone in a group at a restaurant - you cannot cover just the first person's meal and call the bill settled.

standard_form_add_subtract.what: You can't add the front numbers unless the powers of ten match, because they're not counting the same size unit. Rewrite one number so both have the same power, then add or subtract the fronts.
standard_form_add_subtract.example: 3 x 10^4 + 5 x 10^3: rewrite second as 0.5 x 10^4. Now add fronts: 3 + 0.5 = 3.5. Answer 3.5 x 10^4.
standard_form_add_subtract.wrong: Students add the front numbers and add the powers regardless, getting 8 x 10^7 for the example above instead of 3.5 x 10^4, treating it like the multiplication rule because that's the other standard form rule they've memorised.
standard_form_add_subtract.plain: You cannot add two amounts together properly if they are measured in different sized units - you have to put them in matching units first, then add the numbers.
standard_form_add_subtract.like: Like trying to add three pounds to five pence and calling it eight of something - it only works once you turn the pounds into pence, or the pence into pounds.

standard_form_meaning.what: Standard form writes any number as a single digit before the decimal point (from 1 up to just under 10), times a power of ten. The power of ten carries all the size, so the front number only ever describes the 'shape' of the digits.
standard_form_meaning.example: 450000 becomes 4.5 x 10^5 - the front number 4.5 sits between 1 and 10, and the power 5 carries how big the number actually is.
standard_form_meaning.wrong: Students write something like 45 x 10^4 or 0.45 x 10^6, which is mathematically equal but not standard form, because they never checked the rule that the front number must be at least 1 and less than 10 - they just moved the decimal point somewhere that looked plausible.
standard_form_meaning.plain: Big or tiny numbers get written as one single-digit number, from one up to just under ten, multiplied by ten repeated a certain number of times. The repeated tens do the job of showing how huge or how small the number really is.
